[[File:Smoothed Octagon Simple.svg|thumb|150px|A smoothed octagon.]]
The '''smoothed octagon''' is a region in the plane found by [[Karl Reinhardt (mathematician)|Karl Reinhardt]] in 1934 and conjectured by him to have the ''lowest'' maximum [[packing density]] of the [[Plane (geometry)|plane]] of all [[centrally symmetric]] convex shapes.{{r|reinhardt}} It was also independently discovered by [[Kurt Mahler]] in 1947.{{r|mahler}} It is constructed by replacing the corners of a [[regular octagon]] with a section of a [[hyperbola]] that is tangent to the two sides adjacent to the corner and asymptotic to the sides adjacent to these.

==Construction==
[[File:Smoothed Octagon.svg|thumb|400px|Construction of the smoothed octagon (black), the tangent hyperbola (red), the asymptotes of this hyperbola (green), and the tangent sides to the hyperbola (blue)]]
The hyperbola that forms each corner of the smoothed octagon is tangent to two sides of a regular octagon, and asymptotic to the two adjacent to these.{{r|lagerungen}} The following details apply to a regular octagon of [[Circumscribed circle|circumradius]] <math>\sqrt{2}</math> with its centre at the point <math>(2+\sqrt{2},0)</math> and one vertex at the point <math>(2,0)</math>.  For two constants <math>\ell=\sqrt{2} - 1</math> and <math>m=(1/2)^{1/4}</math>, the hyperbola is given by the equation
<math display=block>
\ell^2x^2-y^2=m^2 </math>
or the equivalent parameterization (for the right-hand branch only)
<math display=block>
\begin{align}
x&=\frac{m}{\ell} \cosh{t}\\
y&= m \sinh{t}\\
\end{align}</math>

for the portion of the hyperbola that forms the corner, given by the range of parameter values
<math display=block>
-\frac{\ln{2}}{4}<t<\frac{\ln{2}}{4}.</math>

The lines of the octagon tangent to the hyperbola are <math>y= \pm \left(\sqrt{2} + 1 \right) \left( x-2 \right)</math>,
and the lines asymptotic to the hyperbola are simply <math>y = \pm \ell x</math>.

==Packing==
{{multiple image
 | image1 = SmoothedOctagonPackings.gif
 | caption1 = The family of maximally dense packings of the smoothed octagon.
 | image2 = SmoothedOctagonCorners.gif
 | caption2 = As smoothed octagons rotate their centres form a triangle with varying shape but constant area.
 | total_width = 400
}}
For every centrally symmetric convex planar set, including the smoothed octagon, the maximum packing density is achieved by a [[Lattice (group)|lattice]] packing, in which unrotated copies of the shape are translated by the vectors of a lattice.{{r|ft-packing}} The smoothed octagon achieves its maximum packing density, not just for a single packing, but for a 1-parameter family.  All of these are lattice packings.{{r|kallus-pessimal}}
The smoothed octagon has a maximum packing density given by{{r|mahler|lagerungen}}
<math display=block>
\frac{ 8-4\sqrt{2}-\ln{2} }{2\sqrt{2}-1} \approx 0.902414 \, .</math>

This is lower than the [[circle packing|maximum packing density of circles]], which is{{r|lagerungen}}
<math display=block>
\frac{\pi}{\sqrt{12}} \approx 0.906899.</math>

The maximum known packing density of the ordinary regular octagon is
<math display=block>\frac{4 + 4 \sqrt{2}}{5 + 4 \sqrt{2}} \approx 0.906163,</math>
also slightly less than the maximum packing density of circles, but higher than that of the smoothed octagon.{{r|ajt}}

{{clear}}

==Conjectured optimality==
{{unsolved|mathematics|Is the smoothed octagon the centrally symmetric convex shape with the lowest maximum packing density?}}
{{anchor|1=Reinhardt's conjecture}}'''Reinhardt's conjecture''' that the smoothed octagon has the lowest maximum packing density of all centrally symmetric convex shapes in the plane remains unsolved. However, [[Thomas Callister Hales|Thomas Hales]] and Koundinya Vajjha claimed to have proved a weaker conjecture, which asserts that the most unpackable centrally symmetric convex disk must be a smoothed polygon.<ref>{{cite arXiv |last1=Hales |first1=Thomas |title=Packings of Smoothed Polygons |date=2024-05-07 |eprint = 2405.04331 |last2=Vajjha |first2=Koundinya|class=math.OC }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Barber |first=Gregory |date=28 June 2024 |title=Why Is This Shape So Terrible to Pack? |url=https://www.quantamagazine.org/why-is-this-shape-so-terrible-to-pack-20240628 |access-date=28 June 2024 |website=Quanta Magazine}}</ref> Additionally, [[Fedor Nazarov]] provided a partial result by proving that the smoothed octagon is a [[local minimum]] for packing density among centrally symmetric convex shapes.{{r|nazarov}}

If central symmetry is not required, the regular [[heptagon]] is conjectured to have even lower packing density, but neither its packing density nor its optimality have been proven. In three dimensions, [[Ulam's packing conjecture]] states that no convex shape has a lower maximum packing density than the ball.{{r|kallus-pessimal}}
